metadata.scenario_context: Carly, a single mom working two jobs, has been invited to an old friend's wedding

cultural_axis.agent_1_value: People from Thailand strongly agree that when a mother works for pay, the children suffer.
cultural_axis.agent_2_value: People from Canada strongly disagree that when a mother works for pay, the children suffer.

agent_1.goal_1: Suggest giving money as a gift for Carly's friend's wedding,
agent_1.goal_2: Question whether that a mother works for pay and the children suffer.

agent_2.goal_1: Discuss what should be the suitable gift for Carly's friend's wedding.
agent_2.goal_2: Discuss the concept that when a mother works for pay, the children suffer.

shared_prefix.speaker: Jared, a 30-year-old marketing manager from Thailand.
shared_prefix.message:
Hey Alex, I heard Carly got invited to her friend's wedding. Maybe she should just give some money as a gift. That way, it’s less of a burden for her... you know, working two jobs and all. 

But, doesn’t it make you think? When a mother like Carly works so much, don’t the kids suffer? It feels... wrong, doesn’t it?
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Alex, a 32-year-old financial analyst from Canada.
shared_prefix.message:
I think giving money is practical, but maybe a thoughtful gift could show more appreciation for the friendship. Something personal could really mean a lot. 

As for your point about Carly working, I really disagree. Many moms manage both work and family successfully. Working doesn't mean her kids suffer; it can actually teach them important lessons about hard work and resilience. I think we need to be careful not to generalize like that.
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Jared, a 30-year-old marketing manager from Thailand.
shared_prefix.message:
I see your point about a thoughtful gift, but sometimes practicality matters more, especially for someone like Carly who’s juggling so much. A cash gift could relieve some pressure.

But... it's hard for me to agree that working doesn't affect the kids. I mean, isn’t it possible that they miss out on important moments? It just seems like a heavy toll. Don’t you think?
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Alex, a 32-year-old financial analyst from Canada.
shared_prefix.message:
I get what you're saying, but at the end of the day, it's all the same. Many people juggle work and family life successfully. Kids adapt, and people figure it out. It doesn't have to be a heavy toll. 

But back to the wedding gift... Maybe we should think about something Carly can give that's both meaningful and practical. What about a nice set of kitchen utensils or a gift card to a nice restaurant? Those can really make a difference!
shared_prefix.label: Denial
